# How much machine-written text this tool catches

<!-- Generated by tools/raid/report.py from Docs/Detection/*.json. Do not edit by hand: re-run it. -->

[CALIBRATION.md](CALIBRATION.md) measures how often this tool is wrong about a person, and says plainly what it leaves out: nothing about how much AI writing it catches, because a tool that flags nothing has a perfect false-positive rate. This page measures that other half.

The calibration page also says why it avoids an accuracy figure: any collection of machine-written text ages, and flatters whoever assembled it. So this page uses a collection nobody here assembled, **RAID** (Dugan et al., ACL 2024, [arXiv 2405.07940](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07940)), the largest public benchmark for detectors of machine-generated text, and it states the date. RAID's generators are from 2023. The tells this tool looks for shift with every model, so this half of the picture ages and the human half does not.

## What was measured

- **Benchmark** RAID-train without attacks (`train_none.csv`, SHA-256 `c5467bca6fc7f5c7`), evaluated with raid-bench 0.2.0
- **Sample** 30,971 texts: all 13,371 human texts, and 200 machine texts for each of 11 generators in each of 8 domains (17,600); seed 20261117, id fingerprint `136c179ba9288e53`
- **Engine** SignsOfAI.Core 0.8.1 at `7043e66`, rule packs unchanged, language set to English
- **Run** 2026-11-17
- **Counted by** RAID's own `run_evaluation`, at a 5% and a 1% false-positive rate

**How RAID counts.** It takes the raw score and finds, separately for each domain, the cutoff that flags 5% of its human texts. Then it counts how much machine text lands above that cutoff. The score is this tool's 0–100 divided by 100, because RAID's search assumes a 0–1 range; dividing by a constant changes no ranking. So the product's own boundary and its length floor play no part here, and the cutoffs RAID finds are not this tool's.

## The headline

- **26.6%** of machine-written text is caught at a 5% false-positive rate (12.9% at 1%; AUROC 0.63).
- **Chat-tuned generators 37.5%, base models 12.6%.** ChatGPT alone 59.6%. The four base models sit between 10.1% and 15.8%, with an AUROC near 0.5: close to what a score that knew nothing would do.
- **As shipped, the product would have answered none of them.** No machine-written text in RAID reaches 649 words, the shortest text the published false-positive rate was measured on, and below that length the product withholds its verdict (#59).

This is far below the commercial detectors at the top of RAID's leaderboard. It is also what this project has said from the start. The tells are evidence about how a text reads, and most of them are fingerprints of chat-tuning. They are not a way to tell who wrote it.

## What we predicted, and what happened

Written and committed before any RAID text was scored ([prediction.md](Detection/prediction.md), commit `e007adc`). Each line is judged by the refutation criterion it was written with.

| # | Prediction | Measured | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Chat-tuned rate at least twice the base-model rate | chat 37.5%, base 12.6%, ratio 2.97 | held |
| P2 | Base-model rate under 20% | 12.6% | held |
| P3 | text-davinci-003 between the two groups | 16.6% | held |
| P4 | Poetry and recipes not among the three best domains | best three: film reviews 50.9%, poetry 36.7%, book summaries 33.7% | **failed** |
| P5 | Scanner catches at least 99% of homoglyph and zero-width attacks, with false alarms on at most 1% of human texts | homoglyph 99.7%, zero-width 100.0%; false alarms 0.84% | held |
| P6 | The homoglyph attack lowers the score | mean 20.6 → 20.1; caught 24.6% → 23.7% | held by its letter, failed in substance |
| — | Between 15% and 40% overall, without attacks | 26.6% | held |

**P4 failed** because machine verse settles into lines of even length: `stat.burstiness` fires on 52% of machine poems and 25% of human ones. Recipes were as weak as predicted (12.1%), because they are formulaic whoever writes them.

**P6 held by its letter and failed in substance.** The score did drop, by less than half a point. The note added to the prediction before measuring was closer: the analyzer restores disguised letters before any rule reads the text. What the attack still moves is explained under *Attacks* below.

| recipes | 12.1% | 0.53 | 8.8/100 |

Greedy decoding is caught more often than sampling (30.4% against 22.7%). A repetition penalty lowers it from 29.8% to 18.1%: penalising repeated tokens also suppresses stock phrases, and with them the tells.

With one cutoff for every domain, closer to how the product works, the rate is 23.4% (cutoff 37.0/100).

## Found along the way

None of what follows was predicted. It is reported because it is true, and it should be read as observation rather than as a test that could have failed.

### The product's boundary on short text

RAID's texts are short: the median human text has 222 words and the median machine text 219. At the product's boundary of 30/100, ignoring the length floor, **11.3% of RAID's human texts would be flagged**, against 33.2% of the machine ones. That is the reason for the floor: below the lengths the boundary was measured on, it would accuse roughly one person in nine.

| Length | Human texts | Machine texts | Human flagged at RAID's cutoff | Machine caught |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| under 200 words | 4,990 | 7,800 | 5.8% | 23.0% |
| 200-399 words | 6,463 | 8,875 | 5.6% | 29.2% |
| 400-648 words | 1,210 | 925 | 1.0% | 31.7% |
| 649 or more words | 708 | 0 | 0.1% | n/a |

Only 5.3% of the human texts and none of the machine texts reach 649 words.

### Long human writing the calibration does not contain

708 of RAID's human texts reach the floor. They are an outside sample of long human writing, but of a different population from the calibration corpus, which holds research articles, encyclopedia revisions and learner essays. These are news articles, book summaries, film reviews and verse. At the product's boundary of 30/100:

| Domain | Texts | Crossing the boundary | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| news articles | 110 | 9 | 4.4–14.8% |
| book summaries | 322 | 3 | 0.3–2.7% |
| poetry | 109 | 2 | 0.5–6.4% |
| recipes | 16 | 0 | 0.0–19.4% |
| film reviews | 151 | 0 | 0.0–2.5% |
| **all** | **708** | **14** | **1.2–3.3%** |

Overall that is 2.0%, against the published 2 of 296 (0.2–2.4%). The two intervals overlap. The difference sits almost entirely in one register: **9 of 110 news articles cross the boundary** (4.4–14.8%), a register the calibration corpus never contained, and the point estimate is above the 5% this project promises. 14 of the 14 flagged texts carry `stat.burstiness`: news prose tends to keep its sentences to an even length, and sentence-length variation is the signal this tool trusts most.

This does not move the published number, which describes the corpus it was measured on, and the calibration page already says a rate does not transfer from one population to another. It is the first measurement of how far it fails to transfer, and where. A teacher of a register like this one, journalism for instance, should calibrate on their own students' earlier work before trusting the boundary. Any change to the published rate goes through the calibration corpus and the review committee, not through RAID.

### Which rules carry the signal

Share of texts each rule fires on, for the rules that fire most often on chat-tuned text relative to human text (at least 50 texts):

| Rule | Human | Chat-tuned | Base | Chat ÷ human |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `syn.testament-to` | 0.1% | 3.4% | 0.1% | 64× |
| `lex.delve` | 0.1% | 5.0% | 0.1% | 39× |
| `lex.tapestry` | 0.0% | 1.3% | 0.0% | 29× |
| `lex.transformative` | 0.0% | 0.6% | 0.0% | 28× |
| `lex.underscore` | 0.0% | 0.6% | 0.0% | 26× |
| `lex.beacon` | 0.1% | 1.6% | 0.1% | 21× |
| `lex.testament` | 0.2% | 4.0% | 0.2% | 20× |
| `rhet.in-conclusion` | 0.1% | 2.8% | 0.2% | 20× |
| `lex.nuanced` | 0.1% | 1.2% | 0.1% | 16× |
| `lex.vibrant` | 0.2% | 2.8% | 0.1% | 15× |
| `lex.bustling` | 0.1% | 0.7% | 0.0% | 14× |
| `syn.superficial-ing` | 0.3% | 4.5% | 0.1% | 14× |

Each of them is rare: strong evidence where it appears, absent from most texts. The rule that does most of the separating is `stat.burstiness`, which fires on 46.6% of human texts, 73.0% of chat-tuned ones and 42.7% of base-model ones. It separates chat-tuned text, and base-model text not at all.

Some rules fire more often on human text than on RAID's chat-tuned output: `lex.actually` (4.7% of human texts, 1.4% of chat-tuned), `lex.literally` (1.3% of human texts, 0.2% of chat-tuned), `rhet.em-dash` (1.6% of human texts, 0.1% of chat-tuned). RAID's generators are from 2023, and the em-dash habit is usually attributed to later models, so this dates those rules to a generation rather than showing them wrong. No rule was changed in response.

### Attacks

Eight of RAID's eleven attacks need no language model. They were run, at the strengths RAID's own code uses, on 1,000 human and 1,000 machine texts drawn from the sample. Paraphrase, synonym swap and perplexity misspelling need a model and were left out, and paraphrase is the attack most likely to hurt a detector built on word choice. What follows is robustness to cheap attacks, not to rewriting.

| Attack | Strength | Caught before | Caught after | Mean score | Scanner reports a strong artifact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| alternative spelling | 1.0 | 24.6% | 24.1% | 20.6 → 20.4 | 0.2% |
| article deletion | 0.5 | 24.6% | 24.7% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| homoglyph | 1.0 | 24.6% | 23.7% | 20.6 → 20.1 | 99.7% |
| insert paragraphs | 0.5 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| number | 0.5 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| upper lower | 0.05 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 0.2% |
| whitespace | 0.2 | 24.6% | 23.8% | 20.6 → 20.1 | 0.2% |
| zero width space | 1.0 | 24.6% | 24.6% | 20.6 → 20.6 | 100.0% |

The scanner reports 99.7% of the homoglyph texts and 100.0% of the zero-width ones, counting only characters that typing does not produce. On unattacked human texts it reports something in 0.84% (any artifact, mostly non-breaking spaces from pasted text), a strong artifact in 0.03%, and a systematic pattern in 0.00%. The few homoglyph texts it did not report were written in Greek, where those letters are the alphabet, or were degenerate outputs with no Latin word to disguise.

**What the homoglyph attack still moves.** The scanner counts a disguised word only when Latin letters are at least half of it, so that a Greek or Cyrillic word quoted in English is not called a disguise. RAID's attack replaces every letter it can, and in vowel-heavy words such as *crucial* or *moreover* the substitutes become the majority. Those words are neither reported nor restored, so the vocabulary rules miss them, while the document as a whole is still reported. Treating a word as disguised when every non-Latin letter in it is a known lookalike would close this with little risk, since real Greek and Russian words almost always contain letters that imitate nothing. That is a change of behaviour and was not made here.

### For scale: RAID's leaderboard

Measured by RAID's authors on RAID-test (leaderboard read at commit `84c2ea4`). These are different texts from the same distribution, so they set a scale and are not rows in the same table as the numbers above. Nothing from this project has been submitted.

| Detector | No attack | Homoglyph | Zero-width | Whitespace |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Binoculars | 79.0% | 36.1% | 98.4% | 68.7% |
| RADAR | 65.6% | 44.8% | 78.4% | 61.1% |
| GLTR | 59.7% | 20.3% | 97.9% | 43.1% |
| RoBERTa (ChatGPT) | 42.5% | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.2% |
| LLMDet | 33.4% | 39.1% | 22.2% | 4.0% |

Entries submitted by their vendors sit between 92.4% and 99.9%. RAID's training half is public, so a high score shows that a detector separates this dataset. It does not show how the detector does on other text. That is a fact about how the benchmark is built, not a claim about any detector.

Under the zero-width attack some detectors rise to about 98%. That is credit for detecting the attack, not the author: RAID sets its cutoff on unattacked human text only, so a human file carrying the same invisible characters is never counted against them. This tool reports those characters as a fact about the file and keeps them out of the score, which is why its score does not move.

## Where this departs from the plan

- **All 13,371 human texts** were used instead of 500 per domain. More human text makes the cutoff steadier, and it cannot be tuned in anyone's favour.
- **Language fixed to English**, as the calibration does. The web app detects the language instead and would have misread 0.3% of the human texts and 0.1% of the machine ones.
- **Scores divided by 100** for RAID's threshold search, which assumes a 0–1 range.
- **Both cutoffs reported**: RAID's per-domain cutoff first, then one cutoff for all domains.

## What this does not tell you

- **Anything about current models.** RAID's generators are from 2023. Newer models write differently and the tells move with them. The right response to "a newer model writes differently" is to measure it.
- **A leaderboard result.** This is a sample of RAID-train, not RAID-test, and nothing has been submitted.
- **Anything about students.** RAID's human texts are published writing. The effect on second-language learners (#75) is invisible here, which is what the calibration corpus is for.
- **A cutoff tuned on other text.** RAID chooses each cutoff on the same human texts it then counts against. That is its method, and it favours every detector equally.
- **Robustness to rewriting.** Paraphrase, synonym swap and misspelling were not run.
- **More than one run.** One seed, one sample. Intervals are given only where shown.
- **An independent author.** The same model that wrote the rule packs wrote these scripts and this page. The defence is that the counting is RAID's code, not ours, and that the predictions were committed first.

## Re-run it yourself

See [tools/raid/README.md](../tools/raid/README.md). In short: download `train_none.csv`, draw the sample with `tools/raid/sample.py`, score it with `signsofai-calibrate raid`, count it with `tools/raid/evaluate.py`, attack it with `tools/raid/attack.py`, and write this page with `tools/raid/report.py`. The id fingerprint above says whether you drew the same sample.
